newsitem.title: UK: Dollar rise to woo Japan's bond investors.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rise to woo Japan's bond investors.

text.p: Dollar-positive comments by central bank officials are likely to increase the pace of investment out of Japan and into U.S. Treasuries, analysts said on Tuesday.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing is the latest central banker to weigh in on the dollar. On Monday he said uncertainty about a single European currency could benefit the dollar, as investors move out of marks and into dollar investments.
"Anything which puts a floor under the dollar will be good for U.S. Treasuries and add to the flows," said David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi International in London.
"Prior to these comments, everyone thought the dollar would suffer from reserve shifts," he said. "This will redress that."

Studies have estimated the drop in demand for dollar reserves by countries within the European Union could be as much as $200 billion at or after economic and monetary union (EMU) is launched in 1999.

Foreign exchange reserves are mostly stored in dollars, and analysts say the total reserves of EMU members is likely to far outstrip the amount needed by the new European Central Bank as a reserve for the new single currency, the euro.
The dollar was trading just shy of 23-month peaks against the mark, the Swiss franc and the French franc in European trade in mid-session trade on Tuesday.
Benchmark 30 year U.S. Treasury bonds were yielding 6.34 percent by 1200 GMT.

Japanese domestic investors, such as pension funds, are finding the JGB market is not giving them nearly enough yield, analysts said. The yield on the benchmark 182nd JGB fell to a record low of 2.35 percent on Monday.
"We're looking at a near term target of 2.25 percent," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London. "That's going to be a problem for a lot of the domestics."

Major Japanese life insurers in late November announced plans for foreign bond investments and analysts said the U.S. is a preferred choice. Analysts said they expected between $5.0 billion and $8.0 billion to be moved into U.S. assets in the next few months.
Analysts said they were expecting a 50 basis point hike in Japanese interest rates in the second half of 1997. The Japanese Official Discount Rate is currently at 0.50 percent.

"Japanese policymakers have a problem," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston in London. "It's proving difficult to generate economic recovery, and now they are already committed to a rate rise next year."
In recent months, Japanese investors have been moving out of JGBs into Samurai bonds, encouraged by the low yield in benchmark Japanese bonds.

Samurai issues -- yen-denominated bonds issued in Japan by foreign borrowers -- so far this year have totalled nearly 3.5 trillion yen ($30.67 billion). Of that, dual-currency Samurais account for nearly 40 percent.
"The dramatic buying of Samurai bonds and dual currency New Zealand dollar and Australian dollar Samurai bonds looks likely to continue," said Shepley.
Analysts said overseas investors were finding no value in JGBs at current levels, and were unlikely to be compensated for low yield by currency gains.
"Dollar/yen is no longer a one-way bet," said Hewitt. ($1=114.1 Yen)
